newsitem.title: USA: For last-minute filers, 'TaxCut' makes the cut.
newsitem.headline: For last-minute filers, 'TaxCut' makes the cut.

text.p: It's not surprising that some people would rather undergo root canal than do their taxes. For those of us who don't know nominee dividends from allowable depreciations, filling out the tax forms is like going to a blood-thirsty dentist.

Traditionally, I've set aside two weekends to wade through records, fathom the IRS instructions, double-check calculations and jump from one form to another because the information required for one page invariably has to come from a separate form or work sheet.

This year I got my taxes done in a day thanks to "Kiplinger TaxCut" (Block Financial, Windows/Macintosh). I still had time to do an errand, take my kids to lunch, visit my parents for dinner and redo-the entire return when I discovered I had made a mistake in the first version.

I've been avoiding computerized tax preparation programmes for years. The early versions I tinkered with seemed clunky and difficult to understand. If "TaxCut" is any indication, the programmes have come a long way since.
"TaxCut" makes things smooth and relatively painless.

It has just about every form imaginable. Most of the instructions are easy to understand. You can get a look at the original IRS instructions with the click of a mouse (although those instructions are usually not as helpful as the "TaxCut" explanations).

If you don't understand a term, such as whether a dividend from a money market account is a "nominee dividend," clicking on the phrase explains that it is a dividend in your name that really belongs to someone else, such as a sister or child.
Thanks to the programme, I found at least two valuable deductions I hadn't thought of, or couldn't begin to calculate.
The multimedia version also has valuable no-nonsense video tips for keeping your taxes low.
And you can't help but think of the programme as user-friendly when it even suggests when to take a coffee break.
Unfortunately, it doesn't do everything.

Although there are many helpful work sheets, you still have to add up a lot of your expenses and deductions by hand. (Things probably would have gone even faster if I regularly kept my finances with "Quicken" or "Microsoft Money," both of which are compatible with this programme.)
The only major quirk I discovered in "TaxCut" is that it refuses to print out anything you put in quotation marks.

It also has the ability to give you a major scare. At the same time it showed that I was due for a $1,500 refund, the programme began to suggest that I needed to pay a penalty. (The programme came to its senses as I added in more information).

"TaxCut" lets you fill in your forms directly, or submit information through a question-and-answer format. It audits the form for potential trouble spots, swaps information between forms, and prints completed forms that look just like the ones provided by the IRS.

When you're done, the programme prompts you to make a backup copy (both on a disk and on paper) and gives you a handy button to uninstall the programme to save room on your hard drive until next year (the data for your tax return stays on your computer).
It costs $35 for the multimedia version or $20 for a stripped-down Windows version.
Tax preparation may never be painless. But with "TaxCut," it sure beats root canal.
Some new and notable software in the stores this week:

"Easy Language: 17 Language Edition" (IMSI, Windows/Macintosh, $30) teaches some basic language skills in Spanish, French and German, but also Dutch, Chinese, Hebrew and Arabic. Each language features 2,000 key words and 250 phrases. It also includes a on-line multilingual dictionary.

"MasterCook: The Jenny Craig Cookbook" (Sierra, Windows/Macintosh, $35) has 180 low-fat recipes, including one for mocha fudge pie. It lets you adjust each recipe depending on the number of people you need to feed. It claims to be able to analyse the nutritional contents of recipes you add to the database. Willpower not included.
"Picture This Home! Kitchen" (Autodesk, Windows95, $50) -- This kitchen remodeling package claims to give photo-quality images after you design a kitchen the way you want.

"Realms of the Haunting" (Interplay, DOS, $50) -- An action/adventure game set in Hellston, England. Players must stop the onslaught of the apocalypse. It's for ages 13 and older because of the animated violence, blood and gore.

"G-Nome" (7th Level, Windows95, $50) is another in a growing line of combat game involving robots. This one, with over 20 missions and playable by up to eight people via a network or the Internet, is designed to work best on computers with the new MMX technology. It's rated for ages 13 and older.

"Quake Mission Pack No. 1: Scourge of Armagon" (Activision, DOS, $30) has 15 additional levels, a few new weapons, and "all-new flesh-ripping demons" for the shoot-em-up game "Quake." It rates 3 out of 4 on the violence scale and 2 out of 4 on the profanity scale. It requires a full version of the original game.
(Gene Emery is a columnist who covers science and technology. His Internet address is gene.emery(at)prodigy.com. Any opinions in the column are his alone.)
